introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklets are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (One Hour): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (30 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (1 hour): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Draw a simple diagram of the human heart. *[4 marks]*

(ii) What is an electrocardiogram (ECG) in medical diagnosis? State one limitation of an ECG. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Diagram (to be drawn by the candidate).** A simple labelled section through the heart showing four chambers: the **right atrium** and **right ventricle** on the right-hand side of the body (left of the drawing) and the **left atrium** and **left ventricle** on the left (right of the drawing), separated by the **septum**, the left ventricle having the thicker muscular wall. Label the main vessels: the **vena cava** (deoxygenated blood from the body, into the right atrium), the **pulmonary artery** (from the right ventricle to the lungs), the **pulmonary veins** (oxygenated blood from the lungs, into the left atrium) and the **aorta** (from the left ventricle to the body). Show the valves between atria and ventricles (tricuspid on the right, bicuspid or mitral on the left) and the semilunar valves at the exits of the ventricles.

(ii) An **electrocardiogram (ECG)** is a recording, against time, of the small potential differences (about $1\ \mathrm{mV}$) produced by the electrical activity of the heart muscle as it contracts and relaxes, picked up by electrodes placed on the skin (chest, arms, legs) and displayed as a trace on paper or screen (with its P wave, QRS complex and T wave). A doctor uses it to diagnose disorders of the heart rhythm (arrhythmia), heart attack (damage to the muscle), and abnormal heart rate.
**One limitation:** it shows only the electrical activity, not the structure of the heart or how well it pumps (valve defects, blocked arteries need other tests such as ultrasound or angiography); and an intermittent fault may not appear in a short recording made while the patient is at rest. (Any one limitation.)

(i) **How long-sightedness (hypermetropia) manifests.** A long-sighted person can see **distant objects clearly but near objects are blurred**: the near point is farther than the normal $25\ \mathrm{cm}$. The cause is an eyeball that is too short, or a lens (cornea and lens) that is too weak (focal length too long). Light from a near object diverges so much that the eye cannot bend it enough: the rays would meet **behind the retina**, so the image on the retina is out of focus.

(ii) **How it is corrected.** A **converging (convex) lens** is placed in front of the eye (spectacles or a contact lens). It adds to the converging power of the eye, so that rays from an object at the normal near point ($25\ \mathrm{cm}$) enter the eye as if they came from the person's own, more distant, near point (a virtual image formed there). The eye can then focus these rays, and the image falls exactly on the retina.
*Illustration (not asked):* for a near point of $100\ \mathrm{cm}$ the lens must form a virtual image at $100\ \mathrm{cm}$ of an object at $25\ \mathrm{cm}$: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{0.25} - \dfrac{1}{1.00} = 3.0\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, a convex lens of focal length $0.33\ \mathrm{m}$ (power $+3.0\ \mathrm{D}$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Exposure to radiation can cause either genetic or somatic effect. What is the difference between genetic effect and somatic effect? *[2 marks]*

(ii) Name one example of an effect due to exposure of a body organ to harmful level of radiation. *[1 mark]*

(iii) Give one reason why X-ray radiology is not suitable for examining a fetus in the womb. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A **genetic effect** results from damage to the DNA of the **reproductive (germ) cells** (sperm or egg cells): the mutations may be passed on, so the effect (inherited disorders, malformations) appears in the **descendants** of the exposed person.
A **somatic effect** results from damage to the **body (non-reproductive) cells**: it appears in the **exposed person himself** (for example burns, cancer, cataract, radiation sickness) and is **not inherited**.

(ii) **Example:** exposure of the lens of the eye can cause **cataract**. (Other acceptable examples: skin burns or skin cancer; leukaemia from damage to the bone marrow; sterility from exposure of the gonads; thyroid cancer.)

(iii) X-rays are **ionising radiation**, and the cells of a fetus divide very rapidly and are therefore extremely sensitive to damage: exposure can cause mutations, malformations, and a risk of cancer later in life. (Ultrasound is used instead, because it is non-ionising and safe.)
